questions.q: According to the central limit theorem, what happens to the distribution of sample means as the sample size n grows?
options: It becomes more skewed, like the original data
It approaches a normal shape, whatever the shape of the original data (given finite variance)
It stays exactly the same shape as the population
questions.explain: The sampling distribution of the mean tends toward a normal distribution as n increases, for independent observations with finite variance.

questions.q: A population has standard deviation 40. What is the predicted standard deviation of the sample mean for n = 100?
questions.explain: The spread of the sample mean is sigma / sqrt(n) = 40 / 10 = 4, which matched the simulated 4.07.

questions.q: By what factor do you need to multiply your sample size to cut the spread of the sample mean in half?
questions.explain: Because the spread shrinks with the square root of n, quadrupling n halves it.

questions.q: In the simulation, the individual order values were skewed. What does the CLT say about the shape of individual order values once you take larger samples?
options: Nothing changes: the theorem is about the distribution of averages, and individual values stay skewed
questions.explain: Averaging changes the sampling distribution of the mean, not the distribution of the raw data.

questions.q: Which situation is a genuine warning that the simple CLT may not apply?
options: Data with a mild right skew and n = 200
Independent observations from a log-normal distribution with n = 1000
Heavy-tailed data with no finite variance, such as the Cauchy distribution
Data drawn with a fixed random seed
questions.explain: The CLT requires a finite variance. Cauchy sample means do not settle down however large n gets.
